Square $AXYZ$ is inscribed in equiangular hexagon $ABCDEF$ with $X$ on $\overline{BC}$, $Y$ on $\overline{DE}$, and $Z$ on $\overline{EF}$. Suppose that $AB=40$, and $EF=41(\sqrt{3}-1)$. What is the side-length of the square?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: The image shows an equiangular hexagon ABCDEF, with AB and ED as horizontal sides, A at the lower left and B at the lower right, X on side BC, Y on side DE, Z on side EF, and the dashed quadrilateral AXYZ is an inscribed square. Establish coordinates according to the directions in the figure: let the directions of the sides of the equiangular hexagon be successively 0°, 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°. Take A=(0,0), B=(40,0). Let t=BX, then because the direction of BC is 60°, X=(40+t/2, sqrt(3)t/2). In the square, vector AZ is obtained by rotating vector AX counterclockwise by 90°, so AZ=(-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+t/2), hence Z=(-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+t/2), Y=X+AZ=(40+t/2-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+(1+sqrt(3))t/2). Let e=EF=41(sqrt(3)-1), f=AF. From the directions, F=(-f/2, sqrt(3)f/2), E=F+(e/2, sqrt(3)e/2). Because Z is on the line containing EF, and the slope of EF is sqrt(3), substituting point Z gives sqrt(3)f=40+2t. Also because Y is on the horizontal side DE, y_Y=y_E=sqrt(3)(f+e)/2, that is, 40+(1+sqrt(3))t/2=sqrt(3)(f+e)/2. Multiplying both sides by 2 and substituting sqrt(3)f=40+2t gives 80+(1+sqrt(3))t=40+2t+sqrt(3)e, therefore 40+(sqrt(3)-1)t=sqrt(3)e. Substituting e=41(sqrt(3)-1), solve to get t=21sqrt(3)-20. The side length of the square is |AX|=sqrt((40+t/2)^2+(sqrt(3)t/2)^2)=sqrt(1600+40t+t^2). Substituting t=21sqrt(3)-20 gives the square of the side length as 2523=841*3, so the side length is 29sqrt(3).

In triangle ABX, the angle between BA and BX is 120°, so the square side s=AX will later satisfy s^2=40^2+t^2-2(40)(t)cos120=1600+40t+t^2. Now determine t from the given EF length. From X on BC, the vertical rise from B to X is sqrt(3)t/2. Since YZ is parallel to AX, the vertical difference from Z to Y equals the same rise sqrt(3)t/2. The line EF makes a 60° angle with the horizontal, so the distance ZE along EF needed to rise from Z to the horizontal line through Y is t. Next find FZ: F lies on side AF, which is a 120° ray from A, while FZ lies along a 60° ray. Using the square projection AZ=(-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+t/2), solve the two 60° projection equations for the distance FZ, giving FZ=(40-t)/sqrt(3). Therefore EF=FZ+ZE=(40-t)/sqrt(3)+t. Set this equal to 41(sqrt(3)-1), solve t=21sqrt(3)-20, and substitute into s^2=1600+40t+t^2 to get s=29sqrt(3).

Along EF, which makes a 60° angle with the horizontal, the segment ZE needed to rise this amount has length t. Next find FZ. The square vector AZ is AX rotated 90°, so AZ=(-√3 t/2, 40+t/2). Also F lies on the 120° ray from A, and FZ lies on a 60° ray. Solving the two projection equations gives FZ=(40-t)/√3. Therefore EF=FZ+ZE=(40-t)/√3+t. Given EF=41(√3-1), we get (40-t)/√3+t=41(√3-1). Establish coordinates according to the directions in the figure: let the directions of the sides of the equiangular hexagon be successively 0°, 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°. Take A=(0,0), B=(40,0). Let t=BX, then because the direction of BC is 60°, X=(40+t/2, sqrt(3)t/2). In the square, vector AZ is obtained by rotating vector AX counterclockwise by 90°, so AZ=(-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+t/2), hence Z=(-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+t/2), Y=X+AZ=(40+t/2-sqrt(3)t/2, 40+(1+sqrt(3))t/2). Let e=EF=41(sqrt(3)-1), f=AF. From the directions, F=(-f/2, sqrt(3)f/2), E=F+(e/2, sqrt(3)e/2). Because Z is on the line containing EF, and the slope of EF is sqrt(3), substituting point Z gives sqrt(3)f=40+2t. Also because Y is on the horizontal side DE, y_Y=y_E=sqrt(3)(f+e)/2, that is, 40+(1+sqrt(3))t/2=sqrt(3)(f+e)/2. Multiplying both sides by 2 and substituting sqrt(3)f=40+2t gives 80+(1+sqrt(3))t=40+2t+sqrt(3)e, therefore 40+(sqrt(3)-1)t=sqrt(3)e. Substituting e=41(sqrt(3)-1), solve to get t=21sqrt(3)-20. The side length of the square is |AX|=sqrt((40+t/2)^2+(sqrt(3)t/2)^2)=sqrt(1600+40t+t^2). Substituting t=21sqrt(3)-20 gives the square of the side length as 2523=841*3, so the side length is 29sqrt(3).
